replies.rawMarkdown: I ran an analysis on the leaderboard public score distribution, and, honestly, the scores are explainable entirely by two binomial distributions centered around a couple lower accuracy means. in other words, the entire leaderboard variance is explainable as random chance of some tasks flipping resolved. Local runs show a decent degree of variance on the dev set with this model checkpoint. While not certain as we can't see how consistent the higher scores have been across submissions, I'm mostly of the opinion no one has cracked anything yet and it's all noise.

replies.rawMarkdown: I haven't trained any LoRA's myself. It's because Kaggle's GPU free tier (especially for L4's) is extremely limited (you can get about 15 hours every week). And I tend to get through that budget on testing my agents locally in about 3 days. There isn't enough infrastructure to comfortably train an effective LoRA. The people on the top of the leaderboard almost certainly have access to GPU outside of the Kaggle free tier. I believe the ceiling for a submission without LoRA is 0.20, so I am trying to reach it. But this competition rewards post training more than it rewards harness engineering (as another user shared).

firstMessage.rawMarkdown:
Hello all, 
It seems that the only way to really move past the 0.17-0.18 score range is to train a LoRAs for the quantized version of Gemma 4 we are told to work with. 
I really have experimented with a lot of agent frameworks so far, and at one point, more orchestration, skills, prompts, agents all become redundant. Simpler agents with good constraints work much better. 
But the only way to break the 0.18 wall seems to be to train LoRAs.
